So `ONIGENC_MBCLEN_NEEDMORE_LEN(r) = -1 - r`. If `mbc_enc_len` returns `ONIGENC_CONSTRUCT_MBCLEN_NEEDMORE(n) = -1 - n`, then `ONIGENC_MBCLEN_NEEDMORE_LEN(r) = -1 - (-1-n) = n`.

So `onigenc_mbclen_approximate` returns `(e - p) + n` where `n` is the number of bytes still needed. For example, if `p` is at `end-1` and the byte is a 4-byte lead, `mbc_enc_len` returns `NEEDMORE(3)` (needs 3 more bytes), so `onigenc_mbclen_approximate` returns `(end - p) + 3 = 1 + 3 = 4`.

So `enclen` returns 4, and `p += 4` advances `p` past `end` by 3 bytes! This is the bug!

When `p` is at `end-1` and the byte is a 4-byte lead (0xF0-0xF4), `enclen` returns 4, so `p` advances to `end+3`. Then `*src = p` is set to `end+3`, which is 3 bytes past the buffer end.

Then in `parse_exp`, when `fetch_token` returns `TK_STRING`, `onig_node_str_cat(*np, tok->backp, *src)` is called with `*src = end+3`. The `onig_strcpy` copies `end+3 - tok->backp` bytes from `tok->backp`, reading 3 bytes past the buffer end. This is the heap-buffer-overflow READ 3!

So the PoC needs a regex pattern that ends with a 4-byte UTF-8 lead byte (0xF0-0xF4) at the very end of the pattern. When `fetch_token` processes this byte, `enclen` returns 4 (because `mbc_enc_len` returns NEEDMORE(3) and `onigenc_mbclen_approximate` returns `(end-p) + 3 = 1 + 3 = 4`), advancing `p` past `end`.
